clue.text: In the event, severe punishment

definitions.meaning: an athletics competition in which jumpers clear a raised bar
from the idiom 'be for the ...', meaning to be in serious trouble and due a heavy penalty

explanation.surface: Someone warns that, if things go wrong, a harsh penalty awaits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the event' reads as 'as it turned out'; really 'event' is a sporting contest, and 'In the' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: It names a track-and-field contest, and the British idiom 'to be for the high jump' means to face harsh punishment.

clue.text: Fred is involved with this crowd in Huddersfield

indicators.note: the words Fred is, jumbled together with the letters of the answer, make up the town's name

explanation.surface: A man named Fred joins a throng in a Yorkshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite: the answer's letters plus FREDIS rearrange to HUDDERSFIELD, a town in Yorkshire, England. 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A tight group of people gathered close together is a throng or crowd.

clue.text: A way of serving potatoes and fish

definitions.text: A way of serving potatoes and fish

parts.words: A way of serving potatoes and fish
parts.note: the surface points to the chip shop, but the dish meant is thin fried potato slices served alongside roast pheasant or partridge

explanation.surface: A recipe note describes a method of presenting a seafood supper.
explanation.walkthrough: The obvious thought is the British takeaway pairing; the answer is the crisps traditionally served with roast game birds.
explanation.definitionFit: These are thin crisp potato slices, a traditional British side dish with roast pheasant or grouse.

clue.text: Shaw's saint, not a sound writer, makes a bloomer

indicators.note: not a tells us to drop the letter A from the saint's name

parts.note: Saint Joan is a play by George Bernard Shaw

indicators.note: sound tells us to take a word that is pronounced like the writer

parts.note: a quill is a feather pen, something one writes with

explanation.surface: A playwright's heroine, no silent scribe, produces a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bloomer' looks like a blunder; it is a flowering plant. QUIL is said like 'quill'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a fragrant yellow narcissus, a plant that flowers each spring.

clue.text: Many in America are without…

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, a large number
taken as written
US is the United States

explanation.surface: Lots of Americans lack something, the sentence trailing into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links the surface to 6-down; each clue is solved alone.
explanation.definitionFit: In speech 'minus' can mean lacking, as in 'he came minus his coat'.

clue.text: Some part of the writer's art revealed by novelist

indicators.note: Some part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A critic claims a famous author's craft is partly laid bare by his fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'by novelist' as the definition, but 'by' is only a link: the definition is 'novelist', and 'revealed' is fodder, giving the final RE.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Paul Sartre was a French writer of fiction such as Nausea, as well as a philosopher.

clue.text: …a thing, a little bit penniless

indicators.note: penniless means without a penny, and P is the abbreviation for penny, so that letter goes

parts.note: a particle is a tiny piece

explanation.surface: Continuing 4-down: without a single possession, just a scrap and no money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'penniless' removes P (penny) from PARTICLE.
explanation.definitionFit: An article is an individual item or object.

clue.text: Judge in German city

definitions.meaning: an ancient city on the Moselle, birthplace of Karl Marx

explanation.surface: A magistrate sits in a court in Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: One who tries a case is a judge, and Trier is a Roman-founded city in western Germany.

clue.text: Daisy enters city from the west

indicators.note: one piece entering another means it goes inside it

parts.note: Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire
the aster is a daisy-like flower

explanation.surface: A girl called Daisy arrives in town from the western side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daisy' looks like a name; it is a flower. Moving eastward, you come from the west.
explanation.definitionFit: Travel heading east sets out from the west, so an eastward course comes from that side.

clue.text: On one occasion, when about to whine, lots of money appeared

indicators.note: about means around, so the occasion goes around the whine

parts.note: once means on one occasion
to pule is to whimper or whine

explanation.surface: Once, just as someone started to complain, a fortune showed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when' and 'appeared' are links, and 'about' is the container signal; the surface's 'about to whine' tempts you to read 'about' as 'on the point of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Great wealth and luxurious abundance are what the word describes.

clue.text: Broke so hadn't paid many close friends

indicators.note: broke, as in shattered, tells us the following words are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone skint never settled up with a crowd of intimate pals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broke' looks like 'penniless', fitting 'hadn't paid'; it is the anagram signal for SO HADN'T PAID MANY.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend the two Syracusans were so devoted that each offered his life for the other, a byword for loyal friendship.

clue.text: Spikes protecting climbing boots

indicators.note: one word guarding another means it wraps around it, so the second piece sits inside the first

parts.note: to spike a drink is to lace it with alcohol
climbing means going up

explanation.surface: Studded soles shield mountaineering footwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spikes' suggests running shoes or crampons beside 'climbing boots', but it is the verb 'laces', as in doctoring a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: These are shoes or boots fastened with cords through eyelets, so the phrase is a type of footwear.

clue.text: Fish sailors first ensnared in lake

parts.note: a luce is an old name for the pike
RN is the Royal Navy

indicators.note: first tells us to take only the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A fish and some seamen get caught in a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'first ensnared' as the sailors being trapped; 'first' just takes E from 'ensnared', and 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a Swiss lake, the Vierwaldstättersee, beside the city of the same name.

clue.text: Goat may appear in Dixie

parts.note: a male goat is a billy
may in the sense of being allowed is can

explanation.surface: A goat might turn up somewhere in the American South.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dixie' looks like the southern US states; it is a soldier's cooking pot. 'appear in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A dixie is a large metal cooking pot used by soldiers and campers, the same kind of vessel as an Australian bush kettle.

clue.text: A mixture of things in Manhattan perhaps

definitions.meaning: a blend of ingredients, as in a drug combination
a whiskey-and-vermouth drink, given as an example

explanation.surface: A medley found in New York City.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manhattan' suggests the New York borough; it is a mixed drink. 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means any blend of elements, and also a mixed alcoholic drink such as a Manhattan.

clue.text: Better letters read out

indicators.note: read out tells us to say the letters aloud and take the word they sound like

parts.note: the letters in question are X and L, spoken as 'ex' and 'el'

explanation.surface: Correspondence is more effectively delivered when spoken.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, the letter names X and L run together into a verb meaning to outdo.
explanation.definitionFit: To better someone is to surpass or outshine them.

clue.text: Guy meets right doll in magazine feature

parts.note: cove is old British slang for a man or fellow
doll is slang for an attractive girl

explanation.surface: A man meets a correct toy in a magazine article.
explanation.walkthrough: 'meets' and 'in' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the glamorous model photographed on the front of a magazine.

clue.text: Perhaps I could be blue

indicators.note: could be says the preceding letters can be turned into another word

explanation.surface: Someone muses that they might be feeling sad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blue' suggests sad; it is a colour, the gem's shade.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep, bright shade like the precious stone is a colour name.

clue.text: You need a key for this part of the church

parts.note: a key, or cay, is a low island, so it can stand for an isle

explanation.surface: A notice says a key is needed to get into a section of the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'key' suggests a door key; it is a low island, as in the Florida Keys.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a passage between the pews or the side walkway of a nave.

clue.text: Word that is unambiguous

definitions.meaning: a verb: to put into words

explanation.surface: A term that means exactly what it says.
explanation.definitionFit: To put into words is to voice or phrase, and an explicit instruction is clear and definite.

clue.text: Artistic people fighting discrimination back a musical

parts.note: the CRE was the Commission for Racial Equality, a British body that combated racial discrimination

indicators.note: back tells us to read the musical's name from end to start

parts.note: Evita is the Lloyd Webber musical about Eva Perón

explanation.surface: Campaigners against prejudice are funding a stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns EVITA into ATIVE. The CRE was a UK equality watchdog of the time, replaced in 2007.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone imaginative and inventive in the arts.

clue.text: Crying, having finally got a reprimand

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of the word it accompanies

parts.note: an earful is a scolding

explanation.surface: Someone weeps after at last getting told off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Weeping or close to tears.

clue.text: Fellow in first class order

indicators.note: in places one word inside another

parts.note: best means top quality
he stands for a man or fellow

explanation.surface: A fellow travelling first class gives a command.
explanation.definitionFit: A behest is a command or instruction.

clue.text: It's made of paper — T.A. soldiers shelter behind it

indicators.note: made of says the answer is built out of the letters of the words that follow

parts.note: the TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's reserve soldiers

explanation.surface: A protective wall is said to be built from paper, and part-time troops hide behind it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's made of paper' reads as describing a flimsy wall, but 'made of' is the anagram signal; the definition stands alone after the dash.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a low protective wall along a rampart or roof edge, giving troops cover.

clue.text: Proportion of house given up by Nelson

indicators.note: something given up is surrendered, so it is taken away from the admiral's name

parts.note: Horatio Nelson was the British admiral of Trafalgar

explanation.surface: A share of a house is surrendered by the admiral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A ratio is the relative size of two quantities, a proportion.

clue.text: Two's about right, that's plain

indicators.note: about means around, so the pair wraps around the right

parts.note: a pair is two of something
i.e. is the Latin abbreviation for 'that is'

explanation.surface: Someone estimates the number at roughly two, and says it is obvious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plain' looks like the adjective 'obvious'; it is the noun, a stretch of flat land.
explanation.definitionFit: A prairie is a wide expanse of flat grassland, as in North America.

clue.text: Real imp, they say, before 6

indicators.note: they say tells us to take a word by its sound

parts.note: Puck is the mischievous sprite in A Midsummer Night's Dream
a cross-reference to the answer of 6-down, which cryptically stands for an article, the indefinite one

explanation.surface: A genuine sprite, people report, comes before something else.
explanation.walkthrough: PUKK sounds like 'Puck'. A cross-reference to 6-down is cryptically an article, here A.
explanation.definitionFit: Pukka is Anglo-Indian slang for genuine or authentic.

clue.text: Imprisoned frequently, I am finally free, almost too late

parts.note: 'in the nick' is British slang for being in prison
oft is an old word for often

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of each of the two words either side of it

explanation.surface: A frequent jailbird says that at last they are out, only just in time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' takes M from 'am' and E from 'free'. 'The nick' is British slang for a prison or police station.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means at the last possible moment, just before it would be too late.

clue.text: I'm narcissistic, so I get made up

definitions.note: the definition speaks in the voice of a self-absorbed person

indicators.note: made up means invented or put together, so the letters are reassembled

explanation.surface: A vain person admits their self-love, and wears makeup to suit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made up' suggests cosmetics; it signals rearranging SO I GET.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-obsessed person who thinks constantly of themselves can say this of themselves.

clue.text: Come a purler, and fail to achieve the desired effect

definitions.meaning: British slang for taking a heavy headlong tumble

definitions.text: fail to achieve the desired effect
definitions.meaning: said of a joke or plan that gets no response

explanation.definitionFit: Literally, to tumble face down on the ground; figuratively, of a joke or scheme, to make no impression at all.
